utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Morning, may I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a, Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, and the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleague Mr. Williamson for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours. I am Toma Fila appearing together with colleague Lopicic and Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the accused whether he can hear me. Can you? Thank you. All right. I will ask the Prosecutor whether he can call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before calling the first witness I have a couple of preliminary matters. Perhaps we can address those. In relation to the discussions we have had in the last couple of days, I have prepared a revised witness list which indicates some additional witnesses that we would call this week, and I can supply that to the court at this time. We have included four additional witnesses, which I am afraid is the maximum number that we would have available for this week. There are a number of reasons for this, but apparently the Victims and Witnesses Unit has some constraints on the number of witnesses that they can accommodate at any one time, for security reasons and just logistics. In order to get witnesses here, it requires almost a week's advance notice because we have to make application to the Dutch government to get visas for persons, we have to make travel arrangements and in most cases witnesses have to arrange to take time off work. So, we have proceeded at a pace which is much faster than any other trial up until now, and even we anticipated somewhat of a quicker pace and we have had as many witnesses here as we could get but I think that this is all that we would have available for this week. So I think this will take us through Friday but it may not go until 5 o'clock on Friday. Additionally, I am providing to the court a brief summary of the subject matter of the testimony of the witnesses who have not provided witness statements, and these are five witnesses that we have discussed in the last couple of days. All of these are family members of victims from Ovcara and these are the statements of Vladimir Veber, Katica Zera, and Irina Kacic which I believe was the ones that you had not received statements for. Finally, your Honours, I am providing to the court a brief supplementary statement of Emil Cakalic which was taken in April of 1996. When the statements were provided to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber the original statement of Cakalic was provided but this supplemental statement was inadvertently omitted. I discovered this error yesterday when I began reviewing his file in preparation for his testimony. As soon as I discovered this error I provided a copy to the Defence in English and I immediately submitted it for translation which will be completed at approximately 10 am this morning. The statement, as I indicated, is very brief, it is approximately two pages of text and it is for the witness Emil Cakalic who is anticipated to testify tomorrow and I believe the Defence would like that time so that they have an opportunity to review the statement and prepare for it before he does testify. The other two documents I have already provided to the Defence, but I can now provide all of these items to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Handed). (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the witness to make the solemn declaration? WITNESS P (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. May I ask the Prosecutor whether the protection of this particular witness also includes the voice distortion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, it does not, your Honour. It is image alteration and just before the witness testified he had asked that he be able to use a pseudonym in relation to his testimony, so I would refer to him as Witness P, and at this time I would like for him to review this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we start, may I ask the Prosecutor, on behalf of the court, whether, generally speaking, he can refrain from asking leading questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like for to you review this piece of paper I have just handed you and, without saying the name, can you tell me, is that your correct name? You have to answer orally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would mark this as Prosecutor's exhibit...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: ... 26, and provide that to the court and the Defence and this would be submitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I presume the Defence counsel does not object to...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness P, do you recall at some point in 1995 speaking with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And on that occasion did you give a statement to that Prosecutor which was taken in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was that statement read back to you in Croatian by a translator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness this exhibit now, please, which we will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 27. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is that your signature that appears on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to offer this, tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 27. Statement of Witness P, and to tender this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the court where you are from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you live your whole life in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Until the war, until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And were you educated there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did you complete your secondary school studies in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed my secondary school on 19th June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Going back a little bit, were things relatively peaceful in Vukovar in the early part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of April I did not notice anything. Returning from the Easter holidays we were supposed to take some food to Borovo Selo and we were intercepted on the way by some armed men and they would not let us pass. A few days after that the incident occurred in Borovo Selo on 2nd May, and after that the situation became very tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened on 2nd May in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I learned from the media, but I heard the story going around town as to what had happened, and tension was extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that after that tension increased even more in the area. Are you aware of any other incidents which were an indication of the increasing tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation was rather tense, and it reached a peak as far as I can remember on -- around 26th June in a cafe bar close to my house, two members of the guards were killed. They did not do anything. They just came to have a drink and two men walked in and simply killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you say, "two members of the guards", what guards are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian guards wearing camouflage uniforms and the insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. The owner of the house in which the cafe bar was situated, Slobodan Jurisic is his name, and he was accompanied by Mike Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge were Mr. Jurisic and Stojkovic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As the summer wore on, did you see any decrease in tension, or did it get worse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 10th July when I left Vukovar, one could increasingly frequently hear fire during the night. The town was virtually deserted. People had left either on holiday or they had fled, and then on 10th July I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the reason that you left in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply went on my summer holidays, as I did every year. I went to stay with relatives in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that people had left either on holiday or they had fled. What were they fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Probably they were afraid because of the incidents, so they left. They did not move out. They simply went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge were people being forced to leave or were they doing this of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Simply people were afraid. When somebody knows that somebody was killed in a cafe bar in cold blood, then that probably causes fear among people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did this include Croats as well as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats were mostly going on summer holidays, whereas the Serbs had their stories about this. They started leaving already at the beginning of May. They went to Serbia in an organised fashion. They would go for three days and then they would come back, so this became a farce so with my friends, Serbs that I socialised with, I knew that when they left they would be back soon, and they would arrange it that this visit should coincide with the time that Savezda, the football club had its matches in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that you went to Bjelovar on 10th July. Did you go back to Vukovar at some later point in the summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th August I went back to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Had the situation changed any since the time that you had left in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 18th until 24th it was relatively peaceful. Only one could hear sporadic shooting, as before. However, in town, there were even less people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You mentioned the 24th August. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th and onwards I was in the basement because the shelling started. Planes were bombing the town, and the shells were falling and it was no longer safe outside the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the frequency of the shelling or the air attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days in comparison with what happened later, it was not very high, the frequency, but it was occasional, and actually that is even worse because it surprises you. One relaxes and then suddenly a couple of shells are fired and people get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that you had gone into the cellar when this started. Where was the cellar located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you remain at your house throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left my house on 15th or 16th September when the Serbs and the army reached about 100-200 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Up until that time who had you been with in the house, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the basement with my mother and grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you left the house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the nuclear shelter in the district of Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you join in the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply felt the need to join in the defence of my city, and the main reason was the large number of civilians that nobody could take care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself an Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did the other men who were defending the town appear to you to be Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just Croatian soldiers defending their city and their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there Serbs among the defenders, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes there were, quite a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were most of the defenders local people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were your duties or responsibilities during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To get supplies of food, water, to transport the wounded, to keep watch duty in this area, because we had a large number of civilians. We had four water cisterns with 1,000 litres of water each, so we would transport food from one place to another, then fuel wood for cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were you located most of the time during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our base was the nuclear shelter in Olajnica and from there we went on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you carry a weapon during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we kept guard duty, we were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you remain at Olajnica throughout the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As the battle was coming to an end in November did you go someplace else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Olajnica until 19th November in the morning when a woman with a white flag came and said that, who wanted to go towards the Serbs and the army should go to the piazza, the market, and those who wanted to go to Croatia should go to the hospital. So I went towards the hospital, and there were very many civilians there. Only a couple of us men, so that we drove them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did your mother go there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my mother was wounded on 8th November when she was going to give her blood at the hospital so that she was in hospital at the time, undergoing treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which she was wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lady from the hospital came and said that they needed a lot of blood because they had many wounded and she was looking for donators, so we got into a car, a very small car. It is a Fica, as we call it, a small Fiat. There were five of us and we heard firing from the hill behind Olajnica, an area we called Hollywood. My mother was the only one to be wounded on that occasion in the car. So we just speeded up and drove to the hospital. She was immediately operated -- the bullet was taken out. It was a 7.62 calibre bullet. That is how she was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you elaborate a little bit on what the situation was at the hospital when you arrived there on 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 19th when we arrived at the hospital, according to my estimate, there were more than 1,000 civilians. I went to see my mother. She was lying there, and all these wounded and civilians and doctors were gathered there. They were standing on the steps and in the ground floor. It was very crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital on 19th, to your knowledge was the JNA already there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived, I only saw one soldier standing there, but I went inside immediately to see my mother. So that I did not see them. But later on, around 1 or 2 in the afternoon, the rumour spread that some JNA officers had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see these officers personally at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th? No. I did not see any in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the night between 19th and 20th, what was going on in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening of 19th some Chetniks barged in. Among them was one who was looking for his brother. This was on 19th at night and I heard some shots being fired around the hospital. Our people were sitting on chairs, sleeping, talking and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were you throughout that night? (9:45 am)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night either talking to my mother or a couple of metres away from her, sitting on a chair and drowsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the morning of 20th, what happened at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20th in the morning some JNA officers came in and called out names from a list to be taken out. There was an officer with a bag, and he stuck a biro into the wound of one of the soldiers who was wounded in the leg so he cried out in pain and then he was taken out as well. When they were taken out they said that all the men from 16-60 and all those who were mobile, including the wounded with crutches, had to go out. When we got out we stood up against the wall, we formed two lines against the wall and Sljivancanin spoke to us, saying that none of this should have happened. We were searched, I was searched three times, and then we boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness an item which has previously been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 8, admitted as Prosecutor's Exhibit 8. If you can, I would like for him to display this on the ELMO, please. If you could turn to the second photograph, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And using the projector which is to your right side, if you can point out any items which may be relevant to what you have testified about in regard to where you were taken out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came in this side. This is -- and then we were lined up against this wall, Sljivancanin was standing here somewhere, next to him was Radic, and then the buses were parked here in this street, Gunduliceva Street. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to the second photograph from the rear, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the area we were led to. I was standing somewhere here. Sljivancanin was here, and Radic here, and all this was full of soldiers and Chetniks, and we were searched here, and then we went over there to climb the buses. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you use the term, "Chetniks", what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they have mixed uniforms, they have beards, they carry the insignia either of the White Eagles, Kokades, and fur hats, those are the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do people that you refer to as, "Chetniks", have a certain political ideology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Nationalists. They are Serb nationalists and extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this a term that you use to refer to all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you were outside and you were made to assemble along this wall, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sljivancanin spoke to us, saying that we should not have done this and that. He issued orders to Captain Radic, and then he carried out those orders, or rather passed them on to soldiers who were searching us. We were on the right-hand side, and the women were on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And how was that search conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were searched thoroughly. Any hard object was taken away, even pens and pencils. Anything that was hard was taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was conducting the searches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA soldiers were searching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you or the other men that were assembled in this driveway armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were all wearing civilian clothes and without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Among this group of people that were out there, were there wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were, quite a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there members of the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the buses were located on Gunduliceva Street. How many buses did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure that there were five. I am not sure about the sixth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did you come to get on the bus? What were the circumstances under which you did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After having been searched we got on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you told to get on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you directed to any particular bus or just told to get on the buses in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They told each one of us which bus we should get on to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And which bus did you get on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the one but last and I went to the back. I got in at the back door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe the buses at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were ordinary buses. They were all coloured in olive green.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did they appear to be civilian buses to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, military buses. Military, military buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you know any other persons that were on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my bus there was Franjo Nadj, Mikalic, there were a number of Simunovics, and so on. I did not know many people by name, but rather by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there a guard on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a driver and a JNA soldier under arms as a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where did the buses go from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They passed the market across the bridge to the children's infirmary, then in Kras Street, then straight to the fairground, to the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would request that we show a video to the witness which is -- excuse me just a moment, your Honour. (Pause). Your Honour, I do not believe that this has previously been tendered. It is the video which was shown in part during Mr. Niemann's opening statement. It is the videotape which is entitled, "Vukovar, Ovcara incident", and which tracks the route from the hospital. So I would like to show that at this time. The portion from the hospital to the JNA barracks, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? Thank you. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness P, if you can, as this tape is playing just describe for the court what you are viewing on your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe this is the incorrect portion. If we can... it would be at the very beginning of the tape. How long did you wait on the buses before leaving the hospital after you got on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About half an hour. In fact, we were waiting for these five or six buses to be filled. So that everybody would be searched and then board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Once you got on the buses, did anything happen to you at the hospital before you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I could see they only searched people and took them to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. At this time I believe the video is ready, and so if you can, again, just comment on this as it plays and indicate to the Chamber exactly what we are viewing. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the main entrance to the Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this located on Gunduliceva Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This is -- I forget what the street name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But it is the opposite side from Gunduliceva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes, the opposite side. This is the inside of the compound. That is the yard. This is the wall and the driveway where we stood and where we were searched and then from there boarded the buses. This is the interior of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Which floor of the hospital is this, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is in the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at the time that you were there on 19th, what parts of the hospital were being used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the ground floor and the basement because the upper floors were either shelled or destroyed. This is again the interior of the hospital. This is the door by which we exited. This is the same door from the other side. This is where we came out. This is where the soldiers and the Chetniks stood and we stood against a wall. That is where they took us to the buses. This is the view from Gunduliceva Street. That is where they brought us out. Then we took that street for the... This is Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this the direction in which you travelled on the 20th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the direction in which we travelled. This is where the buses drove us. Here we passed a marketplace and then across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this bridge crosses what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It crosses the Vuka River. Then we crossed the bridge, and here we turned right into Kraseva Street. We continued on Kraseva and up. Then we arrived at the intersection with Ognjen Prica Street and then continued on towards the fairgrounds. This is the fairgrounds street. Yes. This is a bird's eye view of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what is indicated by the rear entrance is the place where you exited. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can stop the video and just go back just a little bit and pause there, if you can go back just a little bit... okay, at that point, that is good. Stop. Looking at that, can you see the area of Oranica displayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right next to the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe where it is perhaps a little better, because unfortunately we are not able to see with the pointer on that. In relation to the river, perhaps, and where it appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the Vuka River, let us say from the bottom bridge, that was the former SDK building and then the bus station and then the Olajnica neighbourhood. On the left-hand side of the Vuka River there is this green patch and then the buildings of Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And there does appear to be rather tall buildings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were seven or eight storey buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, and if we can just run the tape again. (Video played) If we can stop the tape here just for a moment, do you see indicated on here where your home was located in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to point to it but I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. We can go ahead and run the tape, then. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the entrance through which we entered the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can stop it right there for a moment, do you recognise this location that is indicated here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the inside the compound of the JNA barracks and the buses came to be parked in a semicircle over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at this point we can stop the tape for a moment. And your Honours, at this time I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened when the buses arrived at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were parked in a semicircle and there were a lot of Chetniks and military, different uniforms. And the Chetniks had taken the shovels and there were -- would break off the handles. Then I heard them sharpening their knives. They were walking around, they were taking pictures with their -- with knives between their teeth and sometimes some of them would try to board the buses but the guards would not let them go past the stairwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there any threats made to the people on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They entered and threatened. One of them came on and he said, "do not worry. I only cut off ears and noses", another one came on and said, "what did you need all this for", and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were you feeling at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was frightened, naturally. I felt fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did you think was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not think that anything bad would happen to us, but I was in fear of these savages around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did the buses stay at the JNA barracks, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three hours. That was my sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you checking your watch during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of what time of day this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around 12 o'clock or 1 o'clock, maybe even later. I did not have a clear sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a place called Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where is it located in relation to the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the road. Maybe diagonally across.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is in close proximity to the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Less than 3 minutes on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point in time did the buses leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Captain Radic boarded the buses and read out the names from some list that he had, then these people would get off the buses and would enter another bus. Meanwhile, they were savagely beaten by the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have made reference a couple of times to Major Sljivancanin and Captain Radic. How did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about Sljivancanin, how I knew who he was, but I knew immediately. I think that he introduced himself, and Sljivancanin addressed Radic as, "Captain Radic".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when had this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the hospital. At the hospital Sljivancanin addressed Radic as, "Captain Radic", and Radic entered the buses at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that Captain Radic had read names and people got off the buses. How long was it after that, if you have any idea, before the buses left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about half an hour to an hour is when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did the buses go when they left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Negoslavci, and turned to the left on an asphalt road through the tilled fields towards Ovcara and there we arrived in front of the hangar at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this part of the trip from the JNA barracks to Ovcara, did you still have guards on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The same guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness the video from the barracks to Ovcara, please. This is the exhibit that we have previously tendered as Exhibit 28. Again, Witness P, if you can just describe what we are seeing as the video runs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. (Video played) This is an aerial shot, and this is the road to Negoslavci. That is where the arrow is pointing. Then we went along that road and then there will be a left turn coming up. Yes. We turned to the left. This is the asphalt road among the fields. We turned here and then there was a quick turn to the right and to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And if we can stop the tape at this point, and then we will pick up with the next segment, I believe. I am sorry, that is all we need of the tape. Now I would like for the witness to be shown a series of maps which we will mark individually, if these can be pulled up on the computer monitor, which also depict the same route. The first map that I would like to display, I believe, is, for the purposes of the technical crew, is identified as B31. We would mark this map as Prosecutor's Exhibit 29. Witness P, can you indicate what is depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of Vukovar. We see that along the Danube River there is the hospital, then the JNA barracks, and then the road to Negoslavci. This is the road through the fields and then this small intersection that -- turn in the road and then the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can display the next map, which is identified as B37 for the technical crew, and we would mark that as Prosecutor's Exhibit 30. Can you tell us what this map shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is also a map with marked sites of the hospital, the bridge, the Vuka River which we crossed, and then through the streets until we turned into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, now, if we can see B36 which we will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a diagram showing the Vukovar hospital. We left by the rear entrance. This is where the buses were parked in Gunduliceva Street and then we left by that street to the barracks and this is -- yes, the main entrance to the hospital at Jevola Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe I made an error, I think that should be Prosecutor's Exhibit 31. We now move to map B35 which I will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 32: can you describe what is shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a section of the road between the hospital and just across the bridge past the marketplace. What you can see there is this settlement of neighbourhood of Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And again, you are unable to point there where we can see. Can you describe where Olajnica is located on here, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we have the hospital, and the yellow line is the road that we took. When the yellow line reaches the blue area, that is the Vuka River and the bridge across the Vuka River. Across from it is the SDK building, the former SDK, and just above there is the bus station and to the left of it the two larger framed areas is the Olajnica settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that it was located between the Vuka River and the green square park area up in the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this Olajnica area is where you were living; correct? Or this is where you were in the shelter during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war, yes. Yes. During the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you have any idea how far approximately that is from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you take the small streets in normal conditions, less than five minutes. In a straight line, maybe 200 metres, tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. At this time I would like to display map B34, which I will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 33. Can you describe what this depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Here we cross the river -- the bridge on the Vuka River. Then we pass the workers' hall, the old bank, the children's infirmary and then to the Josip Kras Street. Then we follow this street all the way until the intersection with the Ognjen Prica Street and we continue along the fairground street, or Sajmiste Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, if we can now see number B33 which is marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Sajmiste or fairground street until we turn off into the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I know that it is not clearly depicted on this map, but can you describe where the Velepromet facility is located in relation to the barracks ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the street -- I do not know exactly, whether it is a little bit up the street or down the street where this yellow circle is, it would be right across from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, and if we can now see B37, please -- I am sorry. I think we have already seen that one. It would be B32. I would mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we have the barracks, then the road to Negoslavci, then the turn off through the fields, the asphalt road, and that is where we turn to the small intersection and then in the direction of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at this time, your Honour, I would tender these exhibits as numbers 29 through 35, and I have hard copies of these if it is necessary to enter those for evidentiary purposes. For the assistance of the Registry, they are in the same order in which we went through. Now, when the buses arrived at the Ovcara hangar, what did you observe occurring there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There people were taken out of the bus one by one and he would have to pass a gauntlet of people and that is where the Chetniks would beat them and were taking their jackets, away their documents, money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe a little more what you mean by, "a gauntlet"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the front of the bus or next to the entrance there would be about 10 Chetniks on one side and about 10 Chetniks on the other side, so he had to pass by them and as he was doing so he was being beaten by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe this from the bus that you were on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I approached I saw it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did all of the buses unload the men at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The buses were going one by one and the men were also walking one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that everyone had to run through this gauntlet. Did this happen to you as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just like everybody else I had to go through it and they beat me and before I entered the hangar I had to turn over the money, the documents in my jacket. Then I entered the hangar and there another group of Chetniks waited for us there and they continued to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were they beating you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all kinds of things. With the handles that they prepared there, with the chains, with batons; they were even taking away crutches from the wounded and they beat people with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you injured as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was hit in the eyebrow. A Chetnik wanted to break my glasses so he hit me with a police baton. I still have a scar from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were your glasses broken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What else was going on in the hangar while you were in there? Can you describe what the general situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing in an area where there was hay and each one of us was beaten as we went in, and then the local Chetniks went around saying things, making up things, saying that the younger boys had killed children, so they would beat them. Then they would say, accuse someone of having been a sniper and beat him, then a Montenegrin Chetnik came and asked whether there were any Albanians. One person answered and he beat him so badly until he almost died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge was anyone else seriously injured or killed as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for this Albanian, another man was brutally beaten who also did not give any signs of life afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was beating the people in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them, whoever were there, but the Chetniks were the most brutal. Both local ones and those from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any JNA soldiers at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some JNA soldiers, and a number of JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you know many of the people who were in the hangar being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew most of them, as I said, by sight, and I knew quite a number by name as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to show another video to Witness P and I would mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 36, and this is a video which was made in the hospital on the night between 19th and 20th, and just see if he can identify any of the persons that are depicted on this video that he saw later at Ovcara. This is a tape of several minutes, and so again, if you can just describe what we are seeing as we see it? And if you see anyone that you know, if you would point them out and we can stop the tape at that point. (video played) Can you describe what this is showing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the interior of the hospital, and the wounded. Stop. This man was taken out when I said that they read out names, several names from the list. I did not see him at Ovcara. His name is Stipo Sotinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe which man you are talking about, because again, unfortunately, you are not able to point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are three of them in the bed. He is wearing a white shirt with a moustache and a bandage on his eye. He is bald. He is on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: All right, if we can roll it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop please. Here, where the sign is, so one cannot see very well, the sign of the ICTY, if you can move that sign which is in the right-hand corner -- there. Yes. That man in a white coat, he was the other person, Damjan Samardzic, who was beaten to death at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop. Can you stop? This young man, to the left, the one who is sitting and who is holding onto the bench, in a black jacket with a white lining, his name is Damir Kovacic. He was wounded in the chest and he was brutally beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you see anyone else in that photograph that you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is Kacic, Igor. We can play the tape until I see his face better. Will you play the tape, please, for his face to show? Stop. That is Igor Kacic. He was 16 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you indicate which person he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is just next to Kovacic. He is the tallest in this shot. He is standing up. He is the tallest there. He has a purple-ish jacket with a white T-shirt underneath and he has a fringe over his forehead, so the tallest man standing on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, if we can roll the tape some more. I am sorry, Igor Kacic you did see at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw him at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There we can see Igor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know where you were in relation to where he was standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when this was being filmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Or during that evening, yes. If you recognise any of these places where you might have been, and if we can stop it here for just a moment, if you can answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night with them with Damir and Igor. Nearby there was a chair where I slept that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. Again, at this point, do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That man was seen at Ovcara as well. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, it can run again. Your Honours, there is some commentary involved in the tape as well as some interviews so we have taken the sound out of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this young man too at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. We can start again please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop please. I saw this man, the one in the white coat, and the one in a lilac sweater with his arm in a sling. His surname is, "Popovske". I do not know his first name and I do not know the name of the man in the white coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated the man in the lilac sweater, his surname is Jakubovski? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he had two surnames. Dosen, Jakubovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you indicated that the man in white, you are not aware of his name; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can begin again. Do you know who this man is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him. I think he got burned at Olajnica because during the last couple of days they had used incendiary bullets and napalm to hit those buildings, of course the Chetniks. Stop, please. This young man in a white coat in the middle, his name is Damir Polhert is his surname, so I saw him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. It can run again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There. We can see him again in the left-hand corner of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this is the person with the white coat and the glasses on; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Damir. Polhert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I believe we can stop the tape at this point. At this time I would like to tender the tape as Prosecutor's Exhibit 36, and in relation to the individuals that he has identified, we will provide still photos of those taken from the video and those would be Exhibits 37 through 45 inclusive and we will sort this with the Registry and make it clear which ones are which. The times match up and are reflected on the photographs. Your Honour, at this time I would suggest, perhaps, if you are so inclined we can take a brief recess and then...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Right: we stand in recess for twenty minutes. (10.50 am) (A short break) (11.20 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can I ask the Prosecutor to resume the examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, just to perhaps make things bit clearer, I have spoken with Mr. Vos and I think in order to make it absolutely clear which photographs were discussed when he went through, I would like to show each of them to the witness very quickly and just have him identify those and we will give it a number as we go through. So if I could have the usher bring it through, and just take all of these to him and copies have already been made, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, while I have still got this matter in mind, can you help us as to the distance between the JNA barracks and Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is around 4-5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We will have an investigator who will testify later and probably at the conclusion of our case and he can give you the precise distance at that time. Witness P, I would like for you to examine each of these photographs in turn. The first one we will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 37, and just indicate whether these are the photographs, that these photographs depict the scenes from the video that you identified earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I cannot hear very well. Could the interpreter speak a little more loudly, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And as you examine each one of these photographs, if you can identify the name of the person if you know it, or just state that you are unable to identify the person by name, and then any location where you saw them later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This first photograph on the left-hand side of the photograph, the man in a white shirt with a bandage across his left eye, is Stipo Sotinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at this time I would ask that you perhaps display this on the -- I am sorry, just a moment. (Pause). Your Honour, in order to expedite this and go through this as quickly as possible, if perhaps the witness can display each photograph on the ELMO and then just hand it to the usher in quick succession and we can move through this. If you can just wait one moment until the ELMO is turned on. This is the exhibit we are marking as Prosecutor's Exhibit 37. Can you just briefly state what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man here is Stipo Sotinac. His name was called out before all the others had left the hospital and he was in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, which we will mark -- which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 38?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man here is Damjan Samardzic, who was beaten to death in the hangar in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did this man have a nickname that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His nickname was "veliki bojler", or, "big boiler".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please? And this is marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 39?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This young man is Damir Kovacic. He was wounded in the chest and he was brutally beaten at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 40.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This boy here is Igor Kacic aged 16. I saw him at Ovcara as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know this man's name, but I saw him at Ovcara as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 42.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also, the same applies to this man. I do not know his name but he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know this man's name either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is there anyone else in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dosanja Jakubovski. I think his first name is Ivan or something like that. Dosanja Jakubovski. Those are surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you see both of these men at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. And this will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the same two men. Jakubovski and this other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Damir Polhert wearing glasses. And I saw him at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay, and the last photograph, please, which I do not believe you indicated on the videotape, did you have an opportunity prior to seeing this videotape in court to go through it with an analyst from the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at that time, did you pick out this scene as depicting someone that you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain what this is, and again this is marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 46.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man was at Ovcara as well. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. At this time, your Honour, I would like to tender these to the court as Exhibits 37 through 46 inclusive. Witness P, before we broke and started viewing this videotape, you were describing what was transpiring inside the hangar. How long did you remain in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there for about -- I do not know, half an hour, 45 minutes in the hangar when a local Chetnik, a soldier, came up to me, and asked me what I was doing there. I just shrugged my shoulders. He asked me whether I was in the army. I said, "no". I said that I was in the nuclear shelter at Olajnica. Then he took me aside, left from the door, next to Jekoslav Sindl, who was also there with me. We were guarded there by a JNA soldier with a sniper. He was three steps removed from us, and he watched over us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In 1991 did you know who Slavko Dokmanovic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that he was the town mayor of Vukovar, that he was a Serb, that he had left some time in June, but I did not know his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of him being at Ovcara on 20th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, I am not sure that that is a question which is admissible. I think you had better rephrase that. You can ask him whether he saw the witness, that is one thing, but being aware, of course, could allow in all sorts of other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, I will rephrase it. Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic there on 20th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, but I did not recognise him because I did not know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which you were taken outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier took me out after having spent some time left of the door, I was taken outside the hangar. Kacic Igor was there, me, and gradually they brought some others and at the end there were nine of us. Then we went back to the hangar and they took down our names in two copies. One copy was given to a JNA soldier, a JNA officer who said he was a member of the military security in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that nine of you were taken outside. Did all nine of you remain together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were about to go towards the van to take us to Vukovar a Chetnik came up, who beat Damir Kovacic and asked, "what is Igor Kacic doing there?". One of the soldiers had put him aside because he was young. He was only 16. Then this one said, "he has to go back into the hangar. His father is an Ustasha". Then we set off towards the van and a Miroluub ran up to us, a Chetnik. I had the impression that he was some kind of commander there, and a man with a stick was with us. He was an invalid from before the war, his name was Ivan Najasmic. And Miroluub asked the Chetniks who were escorting us why they were taking him. He is the HDZ secretary, so he was taken back as well so that seven of us remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain outside the hangar, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. About one hour, perhaps. As we were leaving it was already growing dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you have indicated you were leaving. Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were still in front of the hangar we heard the sound of heavy machinery in the distance. I do not know what -- they were earth-moving equipment or something like that, but we heard the sounds of this heavy equipment. We were first taken to the Velepromet, and they would not take us in there. There was no space there. So they took us to Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How were you transported from Ovcara to Velepromet and then to Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a van. We were in a van in the luggage area. We sat on some kind of crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who else was in this combi-van with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were seven of us altogether, and some Chetniks were with us, but I cannot recall their faces because it was dark and I did not have my glasses on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Modateks after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived there at around 7 o'clock in the evening, and we spent the night on a marble table that was used for stretching cloth, and that is where we spent the night. In the morning the Chetniks arrived and questioned us, who we were and what we did. Then a Chetnik came and took me with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did you come to be released from Modateks, after this Chetnik came and got you, where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not released. He took me to a private house where there were mostly elderly people whose sons were in the Croatian army, that is in the guards, and the mother of this Chetnik was there. This was a house that he took and -- or made his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain at this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 14th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And so you remained in Vukovar during this entire period; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time, did you ever have an opportunity to talk with any of the local Serbs about what had happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to me daily and among them there were about four or five who were at Ovcara. I did not there ask anyone except for that one called Savic, and he told me, "they are all under the grass".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 14th December where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Sid and I was there for five days and then I went to Belgrade. I was there until 12th January and then I went through Bosnia on to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before I start my questioning, I would like to object for the record to this mode of questioning. This witness has twice given statements and has never mentioned Dokmanovic, including the Rule 61 hearing. I am trying to be tolerant. I am trying to accept that I was not given the additional statement of the witness, but if I do not react, I may be put in a similar situation in the future and this is why I want to raise this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the evidence which the witness gave about your client -- I fully support what you say, that there was no indication that such evidence was going to be given, and before such evidence is given, there should be some indication so that you are aware of it. I am sure the Prosecution will bear that in mind in future. As for the evidence, in effect, what he said, analysing it, was that he did not know your client, asked if he was aware, or had he seen, and that was my suggestion, he said he could not -- he probably was there, but he could not say because he did not know him. So, in effect, that evidence is of no worth at all because he was not able to recognise him and clearly, it would not amount, I think I could say, to any form of identification. I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may reply, that was our position, that this was no identification whatsoever, and the way that the witness stated it was perhaps not what we expected, but in any event, he made no identification of Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That must be the solution, but if a question of that sort is going to be asked, there should be some prior warning that it is intended to ask the witness such a question because it is such a direct matter, going to identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned that on 19th you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody was taken out on 19th on the part of the Chetniks, paramilitary, soldiers, anyone? I mean of the people who were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 19th most people left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry, we did not understand each other. Were they taken out forcibly by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When somebody tells you to climb on a truck and take -- go to Velepromet, that is forcible, to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am talking about the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether any one of them ended up in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of those who were taken out on 19th? No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Among the JNA personnel who came, did they have the five point stars on their hats? Sljivancanin and the rest of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any five point stars. I only recall seeing --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What? White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, white -- red flags without a star.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that would... very well, there is no problem. There is a tape that exists. Were also among them some local Serbs among the paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were these the local Serbs who know Vukovar as, for instance, you know Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they need any other assistance so that the JNA would move through Vukovar or were the Serbs enough in order for them to be shown things around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was it -- I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that they knew Vukovar. All these local people would be able to show them where the bus station was, where everything else was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I knew, the military had very precise maps. They did not need anyone to guide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just another thing, since you took part in the battle in some way, it does not matter how, who was in the area between Negoslavci and Vukovar during the battle? Let us say in September, October, November, while you were -- how shall I express it -- free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the barracks there from a while back. I do not know who was there. I cannot claim, but it is certain that shells were coming from that area. So, the military and probably the Chetniks. I have some information that there were also Chetniks, some local ones and some that came from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor, you said what you meant by the word, "Chetnik". What do you mean by the word, "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, "Ustasha", is the historical army of the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there such people in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I refer to the history.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understood that, but, were there any contemporary ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the 1941 through 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any paramilitary formations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this also historic thing, or, for instance, what power did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about -- oh, you mean as a historic person or somebody who had some paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they armed formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see a single "paraga" there. I do not know if they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were going from the hospital to the JNA barracks, did you go directly or did you go to the Velepromet and then around, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We went directly to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Velepromet is across or a little further up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand that you did not have a watch, but -- so it is difficult for you to orientate yourself in time, but what time of the day was it approximately when you arrived at Ovcara, and approximately, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. When all these five or six buses, as you stated, arrived there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 2 and 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean 2 or 3 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Between 5 and 6 in the afternoon, just to avoid confusion. Thank you. You mentioned the same Jurisic. He killed those two guardsmen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This person -- is this a person who has some fingers missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is a neighbour of mine. I know him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan. He killed -- he executed a man who he had first wounded and then he stepped over him and executed him. That was on 26th or 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you are -- or were left without your glasses when you were hit with the baton on your eyebrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How strong are your glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 2:25.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You -- after you left without your glasses you recognised some persons pretty well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is not such a bad sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I know, I have very similar. The reason I ask you is because later in a van, when you were seven, who did you recognise? Who did you know among these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew -- I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. If you do not want to -- if there is any kind of danger you can just write them down on a piece of paper. They do not have to be revealed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honours, do I need to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Why are you hesitating? May I ask you whether there is any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of these people are going to be testifying and are protected witnesses, so perhaps that is the concern of the witness, that he is aware that these other people have requested protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you object to his writing on a piece of paper as suggested by the Defence

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Could you please write them on a piece of paper? (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could I see that before it is tendered, please? We would have no objection to that being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you did not see the stars in the hospital on 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. How about at Ovcara? Did you see anybody wearing these five-pointed stars? Did you serve the army, by the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because of my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Me too. So do you recall anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall anybody at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you do not recall seeing them? Do you remember in which bus you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were any of these people that you wrote down with you on that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All of them or some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please mark the ones who were there for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this was the next to last.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which one was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
