utterances.text: If there were six it was the fifth, if there were five it was the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. So fourth or fifth. Please just put a mark on each one that was on the bus with you. Excuse me, are you done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I only have one last question, then. You said that there was some hay in this hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the last question, I apologise. I will not keep you much longer. Would that have meant that somebody slept on this hay or that somebody had stayed there before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an agricultural farm so I do not know what it was for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any machinery there like combines, tractors, or earth movers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was something there but in the very back of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean inside the hangar? I am referring to the outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard some heavy machinery outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions and I agree that the witness may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, your Honour, please. (Pause). Your Honour, did Mr. Fila intend to tender this into evidence? Was it? Has it been tendered and given a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, because I thought that maybe later I would confirm this list with others who may testify. No other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So this would be Defence exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sorry, I have a few questions. I am not clear about one or two points. First of all, you said nine persons -- you saw nine persons who were beaten. When and where were they beaten? The nine persons you indicated you saw in the picture? In the hangar or before entering the hangar? I did not understand you correctly so I am just asking for a point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many people I identified on this tape. If it is nine, then it is nine. They beat them before entering the hangar and inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also inside the hangar. Yes. Tell me, so you -- they took off your glasses before you entered the hangar or in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the hangar. They did not take away my glasses but the Chetnik broke them with a baton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As soon as you entered the hangar they were broken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And so I understand it, you are short-sighted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What sort of light was there in the hangar? How could you see the other people moving around in the hangar? How could you recognise the faces of other people? Was it daylight, because it was in the afternoon? In the afternoon, it was not yet dark. I understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was daylight. There was daylight and close-up I can recognise people I know, and men I knew them. Even if they were further away from me I could recognise them by their voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. So the light came in, entered the hangar from where? I am asking from where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the door, and there were some kind of windows up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. Can you remember how many windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Along the edge of the ceiling there is one window next to another, just below the roof in a line, the whole length of the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Did you mean to say that there were two windows, therefore, in the roof? One next to the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. There is the roof, and then below that the whole length of the wall, there are windows. One next to another. I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And in addition, how many doors were there in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two on one side, two large ones, and I think there were another two on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While you were in the hangar were the doors open or were they shut by the people who took you inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One door was open to the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you do not mind I would like to ask you a question relating to the -- what happened in June 1991. You spoke of the murder of two people who were murdered somewhere, I think, in Vukovar. Then at one point you mentioned that some soldiers were wearing the -- and I quote what you said, "the insignia of the Croatian army". Do you know when soldiers, Croatian soldiers started wearing the insignia of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those two men were wearing the uniforms of the Croatian army and they came to the coffee bar to have a drink and these two came and killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but if I, again, have understood you correctly, that means that those two soldiers were not members of the JNA, at that stage. In June 1991, there were already soldiers wearing the uniform and the insignia of the Croatian army as distinct from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the end of June. Somewhere around 27th June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand there are no objections -- oh yes. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for clarification, we have some photographs of the hangar and this might elucidate a little further on the questions you are asking, so if these could be showed to the witness and placed on the ELMO, perhaps this would help to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 20. I would ask that it be turned to the fourth photograph from the rear. I am sorry, the fifth photograph from the rear and then to go forward from that point. If the usher could bring it over here I can pinpoint the page. Witness P, if you can indicate to the court what is depicted in this first photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the hangar where we were brought. This is one door, and windows below the roof. This is the hangar. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps if the overhead lights could be dimmed a little bit, I think there is quite a reflection on here. It might make it a little clearer. That is fine. Thank you. If you can, could you just indicate one more time what you have just pointed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is one of the doors. All of this is the hangar. These are the windows, just below the roof that I was talking about. This is the other door that was shut, and on the rear side I think there were also two doors but they were closed and there were also windows parallel to these on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which door were you and the other men brought in on 20th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This way, the buses were lined up here and then one by one they would park here. The Chetniks were standing on both sides of this drive. We had to pass between them. On the one side they collected the documents, and the group of us nine and afterwards seven were lined up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to the next page, please, and if the view can be brought out a little bit to show the whole photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the door. The men were standing alongside the walls. The Chetniks were here, and I was standing right here when I was separated, together with Vejekoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Again, if you would turn to the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the interior of the hangar. This was taken from the entrance. This is the other door that I mentioned. Here are the windows. Roughly here was the hay. This is where they killed one man. I was here. I was standing somewhere here. This is where they beat Damir Kovacic. All this is very close. Kemo was dragged out from here and beaten here and as I knew him, and regardless of my eyesight, I knew his figure, I knew his clothing, so it was easy to see, and especially here when Kovacic was being beaten. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And if you would turn to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was roughly from this spot that the photograph was taken, that the guard stood. I was here, and roughly in the middle somewhere here, was a JNA officer. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have indicated early in your testimony that at the time that you were in there there was no machinery in the hangar, though. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could go back to the previous photograph, something like this may have been here at the back, but this is not a machine, it is an accessory. So it was somewhere here in the back. One or two of these things. These accessories. They are not machines themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, only he forgot to describe the officer. I do not know whether that has any significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What do you mean, "describe the officer"? He said that there was a JNA officer standing in the middle of the hangar. Do you want to ask him a question about the officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I thought perhaps it might be interesting to hear what he looked like, what rank he had, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the rank because I never served the army. He was in a regular uniform of the JNA. He had a cap on his head. He was rather fat, about 170, and with grey-ish hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much for coming here to testify. You may now be released. Are you going to call...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you going to call Witness K?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It is Witness K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you what sort of protection you intend to provide to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This witness would like to have his face protected as well, but his voice will be his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration? WITNESS K (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the witness now a piece of paper and I would like to ask him whether the name of this piece of paper is his name, and I would ask him to say, "yes", or, "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would tender that as our next Prosecution exhibit under seal. It might be 46 or 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will refer to you as, "Witness K", from now on. Are you feeling comfortable, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall that you were interviewed on 7th September 1995 by an investigator from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you recall that you signed a document which was the English translation of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask the usher to show him both the English original and the Croatian translation and ask him whether he sees his signature at the bottom of the English original. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I would like to tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit, that is 48, and the Croatian translation would be 48A. Both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Fila? No objection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness K, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the place where you lived most of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please outline quickly for us your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school then secondary school for transportation and I am now studying physical education and I also went to some military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your profession now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a professional officer of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you serve in another army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Only in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you join the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 10th August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Why did you decide to join the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was about 20 at the time. My homeland, Croatia, was in danger. There was war in the air, and I thought it was necessary for me to join in the defence of its sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you register for going into the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zagreb. In the settlement of Rakitje.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you sign a piece of paper, a contract?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I signed a contract joining the guards, the People's Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you sign any type of oath on that paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One could call it that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately what the wording was on that contract?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I pledged to protect the interests of the Croatian state, its sovereignty, its people and citizens living in it, and if necessary, that I would be willing to lay down my life in defence of those goals. That was the most important thing, and then also some rights and duties were indicated of me as a member of the People's Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you paid for rendering these services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received a salary.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Who did pay you that salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long did this contract last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We signed for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you get any training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Brief, basic training.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you receive this training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a place called Kumrovec.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the Zagorje region of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you wear any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any indication on the uniform or coat or hat that this was a uniform of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Croatian coat of arms and the Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30th of September, 1st October. I entered Vukovar on 1st October at 3.30 am.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Who gave you the command to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was given the command by my commander, Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Is he also in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What was your unit composed of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit had 20 men. It was divided into two detachments of ten men each.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you the leading of one of those two detachments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I led the second detachment with 10 men in it.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of unit was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Who were your subordinates, the ten people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were soldiers, just like me.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Are they also from Zagreb, from the area you are coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly infantry weapons and anti-armoured weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what happened when your unit arrived in Vukovar that night in the morning of October 1st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, we replaced a unit that was already in Vukovar at the silo. We took up those positions there, and we protected those positions from attack from the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: So this location you were positioned at was located at the Danube. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: You protected those positions against attacks from the Danube, you just said. Who was on the other side of the Danube?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the other side was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what weapons the soldiers of the JNA had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the weapons they fired at us, they had artillery, aeroplanes, so they targeted us with shells, cannon, and aircraft. They had all the weaponry that they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: At your position at the Danube, did you ever have any contacts with the enemy? I mean, did you have any infantry contacts with the enemy? You mentioned shelling before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We did not have any infantry contact. On one occasion they tried to cross the Danube but one could not really call it an operation or an action. There were no infantry contacts with them at the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: After you left the position at the Danube, did you move to another location in the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this location was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly in the Prvomajska Street, or 1st May Street.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Here at this location, do you have any infantry contacts with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also have infantry contacts with other forces apart from JNA, like paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the difference between those two groups, between the JNA and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference is in the clothing, their insignia, that is the greatest difference.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: From your impression in combat, can you tell us whether you thought they acted in concert, they acted together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since they were attacking us together, it is logical to conclude that they were acting in concert. Logic tells you that you cannot engage in an operation unless you have co-ordination and agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that one of those two groups, the paramilitaries and the JNA forces was superior to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that the JNA had the weaponry and the logistics, so I can only draw the logical conclusion that the paramilitary formations were subordinated to the Yugoslav People's Army and of course they had the educated people so probably they were in control. That is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: You are a professional soldier. When you looked at those two forces, at the soldiers from the JNA and the ones from the paramilitaries, was there any difference in terms of behaviour in combat, their appearance, the way they were fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly in the front-lines were the JNA soldiers. That is as far as I was able to observe. The others were a little bit in the rear. At least in the area in which I operated there was the Yugoslav People's Army, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was there a time when you went to the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Vukovar hospital on several occasions and that is where I was at a time of the surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you surrender? Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me the surrender was on 20th November when the army took over and when they put us on buses. For me that marks the date of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: When was the time when you entered the hospital and remained there for a couple of days? Can you recall that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must understand that six and a half years have passed, and I will say that perhaps it was the 17th but it could have been 18th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reason why you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those moments I saw no other solution. I had no choice and I had no way out.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you the only unit that surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were not.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: So there were many units that surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The entire town surrendered, so all the military who were there at the time had to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: So the effect of that mass surrender was that the fighting had stopped in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that in the last two days there were no -- there was no fighting because the Yugoslav People's Army saw that everything was gone, that there were no positions left, that there was no resistance, so that was logical.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation you encountered in the hospital when you entered it on a date which might be 16th or 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was already a big crowd at the hospital because everybody was pulling back towards the area of the hospital. There were a lot of civilians in there and a lot of children, a lot of wounded. Everybody gathered there, whoever was leaving their shelters would be retreating towards the hospital. So there was a big mess, there was panic and a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you take your weapons into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people, how many subordinates of your unit did surrender together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number, but about seven or eight people.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they have weapons when they entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Most of them were wounded so they went to the hospital and there they did not bring their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you personally wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you become aware that on November 19th the JNA entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them in the evening hours of 19th. It may have been close to midnight. I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning now to the 20th November, were you some time in the morning told to get out of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you recall after all this time what time you were called out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to remember. I think that the time was between 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What did you see outside the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I saw a lot of our people in civilian clothes. I saw the JNA soldiers. I saw their local forces, the paramilitaries. I also saw some military vehicles. I saw the APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened to you personally when you left the hospital building? Were you stopped at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were all stopped there at the entrance to the hospital, and we were searched by the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there more JNA soldiers around other than the ones who were conducting the searches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were others as security.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the number, but there was enough of them to protect themselves from some potential reaction of ours which obviously was not coming. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were those soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: You described JNA soldiers and also others, paramilitaries. Is that correct? Are you talking about paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: You said there were many soldiers. Can you tell us whether there were more JNA soldiers or more paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see only soldiers or were there also officers with a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not look at it personally, nor did I see -- look, but based on a rank, and everything I saw that they were issuing commands, the way they spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: In your opinion at that time, was your impression that this scene was organised or was it chaotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not chaotic. Everything was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see a person called Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was leaving the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us his appearance? How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform, and he had the five-pointed star on his head. He had moustache on. He was tall, taller than me. He also stood out because he was yelling at some soldiers to move along. As I was coming out of the hospital, there was something stopped and so as I remember him, yelling at his soldiers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How many minutes or how long did you see Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- I guess I saw him for no more than five minutes. That is my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: After these searches you described, where were you then taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put us on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of buses? Colour, maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were civilians. Maybe there were some military there as well, but at that time it was not very important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall how many buses there were standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall on which of those five buses you were boarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also do not have a full recollection but it was probably fourth or fifth. I was one of the last ones to board.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were these buses parked inside the hospital yard or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Outside in the street behind the back or the rear entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there guards on your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes they were.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: These guards, were they JNA or paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA guards.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people were with you on that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since there are 50-55 seats on a bus, I guess that was about the number of people who were on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you know one or the other of those passengers on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the name or the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Zeloko Majer, and I think Ivan Gruber and I knew some other people from sight, but since I was not from Vukovar I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Those two persons, were they members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zeloko Majer came to Vukovar together with me and Gruber arrived a bit earlier, but we were all in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there also women or kids on the bus, or only men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no children, there was one woman with his -- with her husband on the bus. Later they were made to get off the bus. There were no other women.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do we know what time of day you entered the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only estimate it. The search did not last more than half an hour, between fifteen minutes and half an hour, so between 10 o'clock, 10.30, we boarded the buses and moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you told where the trip went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers and their superiors did not tell us where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did the trip go to, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went through the city and then we came to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you go slow or fast with this bus? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively slow through the city.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did it go slow because there was still fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There was no fighting anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did it take for you, for the bus to arrive at this new destination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will attempt again to estimate. I think about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened at the barracks? First of all, did you see any soldiers around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I saw soldiers because part of these soldiers was escorting these buses that we were on. I saw a tank, I saw an APC, buildings, JNA soldiers, Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: In your impression you had at that time, do you think that the soldiers you met now around the barracks were part of the same organisation like the ones you have seen at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What makes you have this impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there together, they spoke together, they drove together, inspected the same vehicle. They were mixed but you could tell that the JNA had a leading role. They all carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did those soldiers you just described enter your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two JNA guards on our bus and did not allow anyone to board it. The Chetniks would come to the door. They would make noise, they would curse, but they were not coming onto the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did at one point the JNA soldier came on board of the bus with a list of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a soldier. There was a captain who got on the bus and he read out some names and these people got off.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the appearance of this captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He looked to me to be pretty -- well, tall and strong. He had a hat with a -- a blue beret with the five-pointed star on it. I think he had a dark complexion.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see what happened to the people who were taken out of the bus, according to that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to another bus which was parked off to the side and was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to those people when they entered the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw Chetniks beating one person. The soldiers were taking him somewhere and then the Chetniks ran over there and beat him. He was the only one that I saw being beaten and the rest were just boarding the bus and sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the vicinity of these barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me it seemed very long, 2-3 hours in the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what time in the day the buses left again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about 2 o'clock, 2.30 in the afternoon when we moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Into which direction did you move on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know the direction in which we were going, but when we arrived at Ovcara I knew that I was at Ovcara so that is where we were going. At that time I actually did not know that this was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there still guards on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And were these guards the same as had entered the bus already in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did the other buses which had started with you at the hospital, were still following you, your bus now, or were in front of your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a convoy, and the bus in which they later separated some people out joined the convoy in which we were.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned that you arrived at the place you later learned was called Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did it take to arrive at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give my estimate. Again it may not be accurate. I think it should not have taken more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you elaborate a little bit more about the location. What did you see? Were there buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first arrived at a compound. I think that there were two or three structures there after the left, and then we made a right turn, maybe 1, 2, 300 metres. That is not so important. Off to the right there was this hangar where buses came to a stop. I think that my bus was next to the last in this convoy. When we arrived there I saw JNA soldiers, Chetniks. The ones who were in front of the hospital who went with us to the barracks, they were there again. I saw some military vehicles, APCs, a couple of civilian vehicles, and after that when we came to stop people slowly started getting off the buses one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What did you see then when you personally had to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that in front of the hangar a gauntlet or was -- was created by the Chetniks and people were passing through there. Everything of value was -- they were stripped off, and we were wearing -- the Catholics, we were wearing crowns and that was all taken away from us and then we would get beaten and as we were passing through and entering the hangar, a pile of all these valuables and belongings was growing.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you personally taken from the bus and then you had to run through this -- what you described as, "gauntlet", or were you -- did you meet somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got off the buses, we did not run. We had to first stand there and then move slowly towards the gauntlet and as I was approaching it, that is about 20-30 metres before you reach this gauntlet. These young soldiers, the JNA soldiers would ask us, "who are you, where are you from?". I guess they were interested in that at that time, who we were and where we were from so a soldier approached me and asked me where I was from. I told him I was from Zagreb. He shook his hands, and he said, "Well, you have really got stuck here. I have a couple of days and I am off to Ruma". I said, "Oh, I have a friend in Ruma", and he asked me, "who is your friend? Where does he live?". I remembered that he was somewhere near to the JNA hall and I remembered the address more or less. I told him the name of my friend in Ruma. He told me that he knew this man. I was already approaching this gauntlet, and I told him, "could you please save me, if you can?", and he sort of shrugged his -- he shrugged and he said, "God will save you", so then at that point I reached this gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: After you had to go through this gauntlet, where did you arrive at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived at a door to the hangar. I remember that to the right I heard, "there is Sinilsav Slovakovic, he is an Ustasha", and so they beat him and I passed by and then I started getting a beating. There were three soldiers who beat me. I do not recall how they looked like, what they were wearing, whether they were JNA, whether they were Chetniks, I do not recall any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How long were you beaten? How long did this time last of beating with regard to you, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unlike the others who were beaten, I cannot call what I received a big beating because it did not take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened after those five minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The young man with whom I had established contact outside came as an escort of the JNA officers, and there was also another soldier which is what I figured out later. His friend, I guess, and now I am going to try to quote as close as I remember. He pointed at me, he said, "do not beat him any longer", and then he turned to his officer and he said, "Captain, can I save this man? He is a good man. I know him from before. Can I take him out of the hangar?", and the captain at that time said, "take him out and keep him there so that the Chetniks would not do anything". After that, I was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe that is the right time, your Honours, to have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How much time do you need to complete your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let us have a break now and we will resume the hearing at 2.30 sharp. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I would like to continue examination of Witness K. Witness K, you said just before the lunch break that you were taken out or rather saved, as you have stated it, by this solder from Ruma who was together with somebody you described as a captain. Now can you first tell us what the solder from Ruma looked like? His appearance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was of my height, about 1.75 metres. He had light brown hair. He had a green jacket on him, something like a Spitfire jacket, like a pilot's jacket. As for arms, we called it a pump gun, and he looked young. He was not more than twenty, for sure. He looked as if he did not even shave yet.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you describe him as a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said himself that he was a JNA soldier, and that he was due to go home any day now, in two or three days' time.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, turning to the other person you described as a captain, can you describe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taller than me, heavier build. He had a blue beret on him with a five-cornered star on it, and almost certain that he is the same captain that appeared at the Vukovar barracks who entered the bus with a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: So you have seen this person before, the same day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where were you taken outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the side outside the hangar, next to the hangar wall by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do there and for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stood there, this group, all of us who had been set aside, I did not do anything. I just stood there. I was guarded by the soldiers. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the door open, the one you just left, who led into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The door was open, but I should like to go back for a moment. You asked me how much time I spent there. In my view, it was at least an hour and a half that I stood there outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was this soldier from Ruma all the time with you during that hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the time and when he was not there then this other friend of his who was also a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a lot of coming and going out of that door to the hangar, in the time you have been waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly the soldiers, the JNA soldiers were coming in, going out, and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that there were other people who have been waiting with you and who have been guarded also by the one or the two soldiers. Can you name us these people who were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), Perkofer, Zakalic, Perkovic, that is it. I know that there were seven of us. I do not know all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see Sljivancanin at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those two persons you mentioned earlier who were with you on the bus? Gruber Mijor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered the hangar I did not see Gruber, but I saw Mijor because he was close to me, and he had his head and arm bandaged, and I saw him and he was being beaten, so they stayed behind in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: During the time you were waiting outside the hangar, did you see a woman who was crying and who approached one of the officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what that incident was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where she came from, but she suddenly appeared. There were several officers there and she was crying. She was crying and begging that her son be brought from the hangar because her son had nothing to do with the army or the war, because he was retarded from birth. In response to this, this JNA officer went inside to the hangar and brought this young man out and I remember that he told her, "go away now and you must know that it was Colonel" -- now I am not sure whether he said Ivankovic or Ivanovic, "who saved your son".

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And your impression was that this officer who was together with this woman, he was addressing himself as a Colonel Ivankovic or Ivanovic. He was not talking about somebody else but himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went with her inside and he brought the young boy out, so probably he was talking about himself.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to us his appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. He was taller than me, between 1.80 and 1.85 metres in my assessment. He had some grey hair, he was of a strong build, he had male voice, and I know he was wearing a long soldier's coat.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: The woman you just described, was she the only woman you have seen at this farming location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She was the only woman that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: After this waiting period of approximately one hour, were you taken back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were all briefly taken back to the hangar for our names to be listed, registered.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall just before you entered the hangar, was it already dark at that time or was it daylight? How would you describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was already getting dark. It was dusk. One might say it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How did this registering proceed? Was there a table, and who was putting down the names, if anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether there was a table or some boxes. I cannot remember that, but I know that two or three soldiers, JNA soldiers were sitting at that improvised table and taking down the names. It was quite dark inside. There was a low light, a dim light.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there also other sources of light except those bulbs or this low light you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that the JNA soldiers parked a vehicle in front of the door and switched on the lights so as to light up the interior of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you looked around the hangar, did you still see people being beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not beat them any more then.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the scene looked? Were the people standing or lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people were sitting down. Others were moving around, lying on the floor and there were some who were lying without any movement.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people were in the hangar at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were all of our people who had come to the hangar, and about 100 of their soldiers, though I beg the court not to take me by my word when I give this number because I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: The people who were lying around on the ground, what was your impression? Were those injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since it was cold, they probably were not lying there for no reason. They were probably injured and that is why they were lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you hear any sound coming from them? From those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no loud cries or screams as were heard during the beating but one could hear subdued moans.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: What did the soldiers do at this time? Were they standing around? Can you describe this scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were inside in the hangar with weapons making sure that no one tried to escape. Some of them were outside in front of the hangar. I am referring to all of them, including the JNA soldiers and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: When you were taken out, again, of the hangar, did you again have an opportunity to talk to this JNA soldier, the young one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got into a van, a combi, and we were able to talk. I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ask him what was happening to those people inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him what would happen to them. He said, "Well, they will probably all be executed".

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a moment when you heard some sounds like machinery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that before entering the hangar for the registration. When the beating subsided, when it became quite silent, I heard some sounds from maybe half a kilometre away. I thought at first that they may be tanks, though at that point in time there was no longer any need for tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: My last question to this part at Ovcara, your impression, again, also as a soldier of this scene at Ovcara farm; was it organised, was it quite calm, people were just doing their jobs, whatever they were assigned to, or was it just a chaotic situation? Can you describe your impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall tell you what my reflections are because everything was known; that we would go to such a such a place, we would get out in such a way, there would be this gauntlet. It was known exactly where our people would be put, that is their prisoners, within the hangar. There was probably an officer of theirs with a whistle and every few minutes, I do not know how often, he would whistle which was a sign for those to take over for another shift, to take over with the beating, because then one group would have a rest while the others took over. Then this registration of people, therefore, in my view, all of this was organised and it was known in advance what would be done with us and what their intentions were. That is my judgment.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: This person with the whistle, did you see this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see him, but I could not try to describe him because I really can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Only a few questions to what happened afterwards. You were taken away from Ovcara in a kind of vehicle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Velepromet. We stayed there for a couple of minutes. At Velepromet they would not take us in, as far as I can remember. Allegedly there was not any room for us.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Where were you transferred to after Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Velepromet we were taken to a textile factory, Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How far away is that from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not far. We got there very soon. Maybe a kilometre, but I think it is even less. I do not know the town well, so I cannot really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you spend the night in Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a moment when the paramilitary soldiers or Chetniks, or whatever you call them, arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived in the evening, and then they came in the morning as well, the next day, to Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening they shouted, "what are men doing here", who had brought them, that they would kill us as well as those who had brought us, because at Modateks there were elderly people, women and children, and they were supposed to be transferred to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: After you had spent the night at Modateks, were you transferred to another location the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, the next day we were transferred to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed that day until about midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day in the morning on 22nd December we were driven to Sremska Mitrovica but before that we were transported to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: The same barracks you have been a couple of days ago, the JNA barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall, were there again beatings at those JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was not beaten at all. What I could -- as far as I could see, no one was beaten, as far as I could see. In fact, they gave us water, they gave us some canned food to eat. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, in your previous statement, witness, you did not remember exactly all the persons you were with, those seven people. You now mention the names. When did you learn of the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remembered Perkovic and Berghofer. Maybe I did not mention this in the statement. Perkovic? Did I mention Perkovic? Am I talking too quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. We are speaking the same language, you see. In your statement, among the six of us I only remember the surname Berghofer or Berkhofer. You now said that there were seven and you remembered the other names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned later who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. At the moment you were taken, the seven of you, in front of the hangar. Was it daytime when you were taken out of the hangar outside, where you stood for an hour and a half? So before the registration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was daylight. Only we did not all seven come out at the same time. We came out gradually, one by one. We did not all six or seven of us go out simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand, but when the last of you came out, was it still daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was, yes. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After you came out of the hangar was any one of you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is in the hangar, not in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After all seven of you were outside it was daylight, in front of the hangar. From that moment until you left in the combi-van when dark fell, was anyone beaten in the hangar or outside out, of you seven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not, but it need not be the proper answer. I know that I personally was not beaten by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are a soldier, so it is easier for me to ask you. What colour were the uniforms you saw in the hangar? What types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the uniform, the olive green uniform of the JNA, I saw camouflage uniforms, and I saw Chetniks who were dressed in various ways. They had parts of uniforms, some of them were in civilian clothes, some of them are camouflage sweaters, and they had their typical hats, the fur hats that they wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The JNA officers, and generally the officers. What colour uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This captain had a camouflage uniform, for instance, and these others, the one who was a colonel, Ivanovic or Ivankovic, he had an olive green uniform and there were a couple of other officers with him who also had the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said earlier on in your statement that you had the impression that this Ivanovic or Ivankovic, some others mention him as, "Jovankovic", that he was the commander-in-chief at that moment. Can I read it from your statement if you do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my impression. I can explain why I had that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I am just checking whether you still abide by what you said in your statement. Any defenders like yourself, defenders of Vukovar, did they surrender and remain in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not. I did not see any one of them. Maybe there were some but I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour was your uniform? Similar to the JNA? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry. Let me explain. We had camouflage uniforms and it was a different uniform from the JNA camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But in camouflage colours, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Concerning the weapons that the defence units had in Vukovar, did they have any mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the areas where I was, that is the only one that I can speak of, no, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the area where you were, were you at any time in the front-line from where you could see the road and Vukovar, Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I think I probably did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you explain to me why did you feel the need to take off the uniform even though you were part of the regular units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very simple. I thought that this was just -- I wanted to survive, so I thought that I would be killed -- it was more likely that I would be killed if I had stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the Zengers? Would you not have been better protected as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may be your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor you said that it was Chetniks and the paramilitary formations and perhaps they were not just Chetniks. They went with you from the hospital to the barracks, to the Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that all of them went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is not what I said either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called them Chetniks because they called themselves that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They are all the same in my opinion too. But my question was, did that mean that they escorted the JNA throughout this travel, some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you answered the -- you know, I am trying to slow down. When you said that this was all prepared, that they were acting together, you think that they were part of the preparation together with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that they were preparing it together but I think that they just wanted part of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, your impression was that they were following, escorting the JNA so that they would have their piece of the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you took part in a battle, did the JNA know the configuration of terrain around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since they took it, I guess they knew it well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do not take it wrong, I am just trying to ask you, because you are competent for that, you are a soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. As a soldier I can give you certain answers and not some others, but in principle I did not understand what your question was, so could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, just what you asked them, if an army is about to take a town, do they know the terrain? That was the military question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This Basinger, who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of our unit who changed his name into Harlan Von Basinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know what his name was before the war? You do not have to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would rather not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see a Serb with you, and a gentleman that looked like a professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have been, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any re-examination from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions. One point. You said that you joined the Croatian army on 10th August 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You said you signed a contract for three years. Now, I wonder whether you may remember when you first engaged in some sort of fighting against the adversary after joining the Croatian army, fighting or military encounters with enemy soldiers, enemy combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September of 1991. 10th September, 8th September, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And do you remember when the adversary or enemy combatants consisted of JNA members or so-called what you called Chetniks, paramilitary groups, or both, or were they together, fighting together against your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not see them. They attacked us. They shelled us and then withdrew from this position. That was the way we engaged for the first time. I could not say whether it was Chetniks or the JNA. It was the enemy who attacked us. So maybe it is not important, even, right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But was there any time when you had any fighting against paramilitary groups only? I wonder whether you had any opportunity to -- any occasion to fight against only these groups, or were you unable to make any distinction between the various people making up the enemy combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first real war, or fighting was in Vukovar. All the rest to me was not war. We were shelled at one point and we withdrew and I had no contact with them until Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question. You said that you entered the hospital on 17th or 18th November and you -- the hospital in Vukovar -- because you had decided to surrender. I wonder why you went to the hospital. Normally for a member of a military unit wishing to surrender the normal way out would be to simply to surrender to the enemy combatant, so for what particular reason did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of my entire unit which came with me from Zagreb. I was the only one left who was not wounded. When I went to visit my fellow combatants in the hospital, I was considering whether to flee the city, try to break through, or not. That was chaotic times and many of the commanding officers were not to be found, so the defence was not organised any longer. There were some small groups that were wandering around town in those last days, so my assessment was that I would be the safest at a hospital, together with my fellow comrades and that I would share the fate with them, so that was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. I wonder whether there is any objection to the witness being released. Yes, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one last question if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any reason you were reluctant to surrender directly to the enemy troops? You said it was safer in the hospital. Can you...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a simple reason. I was afraid to just simply walk out of a house into the street. I was afraid of that kind of surrender. If I were in a larger crowd, in a group of people, I felt safer that way. That was the reason. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming to testify. You may be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, your Honours. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next witness is Dragutin Berghofer, if your Honours please. He does not request any protective measures. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragutin Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 29th October 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you live for the most part of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar, as of 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the age of 18 I was an upholsterer, an assistant, apprentice to an upholsterer and that is what I did all the time, decoration, interior decorating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do that in the city of Vukovar and the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have a business in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, for the last fifteen years. Now it is sixteen. To be precise, as of 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, do you recall being visited by Mr. Kevin Curtis from the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal on 16th and 17th June 1995 when you were interviewed by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember that the interview being conducted actually in the English language and taken down in the English language, but it being interpreted to you as it progressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember at the end of the interview the document, the statement being read back to you and did you affix your signature to each page of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at what I now show you, please? If you could just look at the top copy of the documents that I am now giving you and perhaps they could be allocated the next exhibit number in order, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And there is a translation of that document, if that could -- into the Croatian language and if that could be allocated a number, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, looking at the document that is now in front of you, do you see affixed to the bottom of each page of that document your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, in addition to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to the events in Vukovar and Ovcara, did you also give a statement to officers of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, the Vukovar police section of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you recall that you gave this statement on or about 1st June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was that statement given at a place in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at what I now show you, please? I am aware of the fact that, I apprehend that Mr. Fila is going to object, but I will certainly stop in time for him to argue it at the appropriate moment, your Honours. Now, in respect of this document that you now have, have you had an opportunity to read through the Croatian version of the document previous to coming into court; this document is not signed by you, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does have a signature appearing at the end of the statement. Do you know whose signature that relates to? You can look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a policeman's signature. I think he was a uniformed policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the circumstances of you giving this interview, can you just explain them briefly to the court as to how this document that came into existence, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was released from Sremska Mitrovica on 27th March 1992, we arrived in Zagreb, and immediately they took down our personal information, who we were, where we were, what did we experience, and this is how the whole story started. Then we were put up at one place as refugees and then they sent this policeman and I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from reading through this statement are you satisfied that it is the statement that you gave to this police officer in Zagreb on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some things are correct, but some things are a little bit... I do not know. Either he was a bit confused or I was a little bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And perhaps, if you can -- I think you know what that relates to and if you can just tell us in general terms, what parts of it you feel may be slightly inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
