utterances.text: I am most confused about the timetable at Ovcara. Can I look at this? Yes, well, here, right here. Your Honour, we were leaving Ovcara at around 5 o'clock in the evening. It was already getting dark, but -- so the times indicated for Ovcara are not really correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the time that you left Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. But otherwise than that, from your reading of the statement does it appear to be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Usually, whatever interpreter... maybe the interpreters were confused here and there a little bit, but for the most part this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at this stage I would seek to tender it, but I understand that Mr. Fila wishes to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before I raise the objection, just to refer to this time. What time, if it was not 5 pm, what time was it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The real time was 1700 hours, so 5 o'clock, 5.15 in the afternoon because when we got into the van --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, that is not what the question was. I think you said 5 pm for when you left, but what time did you put down there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The correct time was 1700 hours when we left. But what was written down is that it was 5 o'clock when we arrived at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, this is the objection. This is not a statement of the accused. Sorry, not the accused. The witness statement. This is not a witness statement. If you look at the document, at the bottom right corner, in small letters, it is pursuant to Article 151, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Yugoslavia. This is what the police officers take and it is never used in the court. For us it was what we used to call, "the pretrial proceedings". You have a copy of the law on criminal procedure there. This was in the case of the General Djukic, so a long time ago. You can double-check that. I do not see any need to provide this as evidence, a document that is not used in this kind of procedure in Yugoslavia and we have a live witness who is going to testify to what actually happened. Why would we learn about these things indirectly when we have a witness who can give a live testimony? At the same time, I would submit that I am not going to oppose if the Prosecution calls this policeman as a witness. That is fine by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Niemann whether this document had been disclosed to the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Not to the court, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, it is not an OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So you do not object to the -- you do object to this document being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, because it is a second-hand piece of evidence, and I do not understand what the purpose of it is, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. We cannot accept that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I will have it marked for identification, if your Honours please. May it be marked for identification, and allocated the next number in order, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bos, did you comply with the request?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I wish to take you now to the events in Vukovar in 1991 and in particular, around 24th August 1991. Can you recall back then at that time and date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to request to go back to about 24 days before 24th August because I was the owner of two businesses. I would -- I was at that time still working, though the shells, a few shells were falling in the town. We, the locals in Vukovar believed that nothing would happen. We did not even consider that such catastrophe would take place. So two or three days I was loading coal into my cellar and my house is about 20 metres away from the JNA barracks and there was a 90 millimetre barrelled gun pointed and anti-aircraft machine-gun pointed while I was unloading this, shovelling this coal. This was just a few days before this 24th, and I had no clue as to what would happen to me on the night of 24th and this is right after midnight, five minutes after midnight, so I came into my bedroom, I turned on the lights, just to see whether I had made the bed, and I turned it off immediately, and a tank was pointing at me, just about where you are, at that distance, and as I lay in bed they opened fire and you can -- I am ashamed to say how I felt. It was a terrible thunder and a big noise. I do not know how to say this, but it was -- I was lucky. There was a little retaining wall there. Actually the wall below the window, and so I was not hit. So, I crawled out of my bed and I crawled into another room and I stayed in the -- in there until the morning of 25th when I heard some voices and then I looked around. I see my neighbour, Mile Latinovic and he was talking to a soldier who was on a guard duty, on this tank. I said, "Mile, who praised me so well that they did this to my house?". Then he said, "Drago, look. They did that to me too", and I looked, and his house was intact. They targeted several houses between me and my neighbour Slavko Posonjak, so they targeted his house, then they spared one and then two other houses they did it to, and then Ms. Segavac's, and then they took turns between mine, Slavko Posonjak and Ms. Segavac and they took turns for a couple of hours they kept shooting at the house, these houses. And a little later after around 4 o'clock the fire subsided a little bit, and in the morning, when I heard this voice, it was as if nothing had happened. I took a little motorcycle, I left my elderly mother in the backyard and I set off to where my shop was. When I speak of my businesses I had five properties. I had a big house next to the barracks about 110 square metres. The rest did not have upper floors, but they had bathrooms and they had amenities. So, I had these two shops. That was not strictly in the centre of town, and -- but these houses were built well, and they had basements that were made there during Austro-Hungarian times, if not the Turkish times so I decided to stay there. We all had believed that nothing like this could happen and then, starting on -- with that 24th, these shells kept coming from the direction of Negoslavci, Backa Palanka, all directions, so that I took shelter in my basement which, during the war, also had 40 women and children staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just stopping you for a moment, did you have any members of the family, your family with you in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on my mother joined me because my house was blown up with a mortar, so I no longer had a roof, then she came, then my daughter, my wife, as well, though we were not married but we were living together, and my other daughter, with two grandsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were your daughters names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vesna. Vesna and Jasna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened to Vesna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took Vesna by the so-called JNA and I never saw her again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have learned now who took her away and if I have to tell I will, but she was taken away by soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army and some people who we called Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And have you ever seen her since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had contact with a man who took her away but he says that he had to do it. He is in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think you said your wife was with you in the shelter as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did anything happen to her during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She is -- she was the only victim among the 40 women who were in this basement of mine. She was killed on 6th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was she killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, shall we say that the Danube is behind my back and the shell fell in front of my shop. It fragmented, and the shrapnel flew in through the window and hit the wall of the shop which is the wall linked to the basement, and at that very moment she was smoking in the doorway, so as not to bother the children and the elderly people. She was smoking there, and she was hit here in the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, were any of the people with you in the shelter during this period of time armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, but I cannot claim that out of all of us that were around there, 2,000, 1,500, one could not count and perhaps some of them were armed and some of them may have come to have lunch with us. I personally have never fired a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were women and children in the shelters as well as men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how were the people fed during the period of the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, Vukovar was quite a well-off town, and as I have already said we never thought that such a disaster would occur. Well, it was possible to pass through Marice and Bogdanovci, that was the only open way out of Vukovar, because on all the other sides were the locals and the JNA army, so we received aid from Jakovo which was brought in by truck, then there were some stores that had been abandoned. Meat was not a problem, but there was no electricity so there was no point in slaughtering an animal when you cannot eat it immediately and by next day it is no longer good. It goes bad. So, we only had one big cauldron, and we were eating. There were Serbs and Hungarians and Skipotars with us, representatives of various ethnic groups. We never asked who was what; when the shells fell we were altogether in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in addition to having food for yourself, did you also have occasion to supply food to other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did. Potato was very much in demand. There was a monastery there and a church. There was not a single potato. Then there was no sugar. Everything stopped working but still, as I said, there were abandoned grocery shops, so we would carry food to the hospital and to the monastery and in the centre, to the old people's homes where some old women were very cold because they had no heating, so roughly 3,000 people would go from this building, the so-called, "Borovka", to -- they would cover 50 metres to get to my basement and my shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the siege of Vukovar when you and some others attempted to escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we kept thinking about fleeing, but whenever we made such a decision we would hear over the transistor radio that a truce had been signed, that there would not be no fire any more, and as soon as dark fell about 7 pm, the shells started falling again on that poor city of Vukovar. And since I had a certain amount of money, some capital, you know how things are. I had to save it for as long as I could save it up. Afterwards, everything was -- all our houses were without roofs, everything was destroyed. One of my houses burned for three days. At first, some fire brigades tried to extinguish the fire but you know what happened to them? They never did it again because high up in some buildings there were snipers of the so-called JNA and they would target them very easily. So that there were about 15 fire brigade men who were killed in Vukovar. Some of them were even killed in hospital when the cistern truck was hit when it was bringing water to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you, did you recall a time when you tried to actually leave Vukovar, to try and force your way out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I remember this was somewhere around the end of September. Food, we were running short of food for the children. I had a five month old grandson in a carrier. I would never have found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you succeed in escaping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not manage to escape. Afterwards, when I wanted to escape, it was already too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, then later did you then go to the hospital in Vukovar in order to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when was that? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 17th November 1991. I think that all the remaining people from Vukovar congregated towards the municipality building which is 300 metres from the hospital and someone decided, they called it a breakthrough, but there is no breakthrough with the two or three automatic rifles and 150 men, so I tried to go with them but a shell fell. Two men were killed on the spot. I panicked, and I went back to the hospital. Around 11.30 at night on 17th November it was night-time, and there was a drizzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to the hospital, were there other people there as well as yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no room for a fly in the hospital. There were so many people cramming those corridors, not counting the wounded. There were up to three to a bed. It was packed full. I cannot really judge, but there was not room for anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you stay when you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the new hospital building because upstairs it was totally shelled, so I was not on the floor, on the top floor, but on the ground floor. That night I never slept at all. I was hungry in the morning. The hospital had no food to give any more, so I had some, "Babyveta", and, "Laktovit", in the infants' department because though it was destroyed, there was some of this powder milk and that is how I spent the night between 17th and 18th and the 19th and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you stay in any particular room, anyone's room in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From 18th until 19th I found a little children's bed and I spent the night in it, crouching in it until the 19th in the morning, and then around 11 o'clock in the morning Dr. Ivankovic saw me and asked me what I was doing there. I said, "where everyone else is, I am", so he said, "come over here to my office and sit with me".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did anything happen when you were sitting in Dr. Ivankovic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not alone with him. Perkovic was there too, Tomislav. I think it was Tomislav, something like that. Perkovic, anyway. Then there were some nurses, then two other doctors, there were about eight or ten of us in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was around the 19th in the afternoon when I was already with the doctor and these other nurses and Tihomir Perkovic, the doctor's son came. His name is Goran. He kissed him, but also some reservists of the JNA, local people who were working in the hospital. They were exchanging greetings, kissing some people, so I saw, I just cannot recall this moment the surname, but I will remember later on, during my testimony, and they immediately started questioning some of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who are, "they"? Who was questioning some of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, he was the porter in the hospital. His name was Bogdan, Kuzmic Bogdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was he dressed in a uniform of any sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a reserve. He belonged to the... how shall I put it... paramilitary of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did Dr. Ivankovic's son have a conversation with his father when he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once they had hugged each other he extended his hand to me as well and to everyone else, and then he said, "why did you not leave when I told you? We wanted to set Vukovar on fire with napalm bombs and where is the granny", his father said, "a bomb fell on the hospital and she got killed", referring to the mother-in-law of Ivankovic and the young boy's grandmother and he said, "I am sorry that she has not lived to see me wearing this hat with a cockade", though he was actually wearing a helmet with a five cornered star.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "she", is that a translation error or did you mean "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was talking and referring to his grandmother who got killed. I do not quite understand what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that clears it up. What did the father, Dr. Ivankovic then say to his son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Keep quiet Goran, keep quiet and go out. Go. Go", because Dr. Ivankovic stayed in the hospital until the bitter end doing his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you seen any reservists, paramilitaries or JNA soldiers at the hospital prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, maybe half an hour before that, shall we say it was 3.30 in the afternoon. That was the first time that the reservists, JNA reservists appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think you said that -- earlier in your evidence -- that they then started to ask people questions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was roughly at the same time when this young boy came to see his father, then Bogdan Kuzmic went off and this was happening within a time span of 10 or 15 minutes. It all happened quickly. Stanko Duvnjak was questioned and he was sitting in the corridor. I remember Stanko saying, "what could I do?", and they questioned some others, but believe me, I know the person, but if I cannot remember his name and surname it is of no good, is it. If you are at all interested, by then it was already dark, the 19th, it was evening. And we spent that whole night sitting in that room and then I may again be wrong by about half an hour, well, you know when one is afraid and one does not take notes, but roughly, it was about 1.15 or 1.30. Pistol shots were heard. Six. Six of these shots. They were quite far away, but were clearly audible. And then there was a pause of about 40 minutes and then again we heard shots, but from the same pistol. So, within a span of two hours that pistol fired 18 shots. It all ended about quarter past three in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would just like to take you back just a little bit through what you were saying about the people being questioned. Do you know why they were being questioned? The purpose for this questioning by these reservists? JNA reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, Stanko Duvnjak was a policeman in Yugoslavia, and Bogdan Kuzmic was a porter in the hospital. Now, why they were being questioned -- I just heard him saying, "what could I do?". That is all I know about that, about Stanko Duvnjak and I did not see him. He is not around any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened the next morning, that is 20th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of that night when I heard those pistol shots, I could not really tell you exactly how many trucks and buses were driven out of the hospital with people on board, but all night one could hear these trucks and buses. You could hear them roaring off, and later I learned about this at Velepromet which is about 4 or 5 kilometres from the hospital, 4 kilometres in the direction of Negoslavci, outside of town. Then morning came, and about 7 am a tall, moustached officer walked in with a flak jacket, Tito-ist cap, a five-cornered star. I cannot remember the name, because I left that army ages ago, so I could no longer recognise the ranks, and he was shouting out aloud, "doctor, what are you waiting for? It is a state of war! The lightly wounded and the civilians should go to the left and the left, for us, the people of Vukovar, was known as the Sapudl. On one side was the Ivalolarejpa Street and on the other, the Sapudl.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could stop there. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We will reconvene in twenty minutes. (4.00 pm) (A short break). (4.20 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, just before the afternoon break, you were speaking of how this officer came into the room, whose rank you could not recognise, but started to speak to Dr. Ivankovic about getting a move on with sorting out the people in the hospital. And I think you said that he issued certain instructions as to where people were to go. Did you know the name of this officer or did you subsequently come to know the name of this officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I am not going to exaggerate, but a year and a half later I still did not know what his name was because I spent about four and a half months in prison and then, you know, I eventually came back and I was a refugee. I was in some make-shift shelter, I did not have a television. So it took me a year and a half before I found out that it was Major Sljivancanin because at that time in the hospital, he did not have any rank. He only wore this Tito-type hat. He was tall, he had a moustache, he wore a flak jacket, and I only learned later from television what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, recognise him on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was very characteristic type of person. You could not make a mistake about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you find out his name to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now what happened then, after he had given this order that people were to be sorted in this way? This was on 20th November 1991 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Around 8 o'clock. It may have been later than 8 o'clock. Well, we lined up the way he ordered. There was also a reservist there, about 45 years, old, rather stocky. I do not think that I could recognise him any more and I do not know his name. There were also some assistants there, somebody. They took all metal objects from us. They did not touch our wallets or jewelry or money, but only some things that were not supposed to be there, like small knives or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about watches? Did they leave you with your watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No, they did not touch any -- no personal valuables were touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, about how many people were lined up in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to give you a figure, but later on those six buses were pretty full. You know, they had been ready in the street, already sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that were put into the buses by the reservists and the JNA, were they men, women and children or were they hospital staff or can you explain who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were going into the buses or those who had ordered people to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that were put into the buses from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Those -- of those some had their arms bandaged, some were wearing slippers, and as the man himself put it, the lightly wounded and civilians, and some hospital staff. They had like badges, and they did not -- they were not told to go into the buses, but some remained, even though they had those badges. When we climbed onto the buses we were taken in the direction of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what bus did you get on to? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I was in the fourth bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, was there anyone on that bus that you could remember that was not a JNA officer, or soldier, but was there anyone on the bus such as yourself that had come from the hospital that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember some very clearly. For instance, Emil Cakalic was there. He was a sanitary inspector of the Vukovar municipality, even during the war he was visiting civilians. Also, assistant, then my neighbour, Drago Gavoric who would carry water to the hospital and then a number of young men, older people. There were a number of people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, apart from the people that were taken out of the hospital, was there any JNA soldiers or reservists on the bus there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my bus, there were two regular JNA soldiers, and I think it was similar in the other buses too, that were travelling together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, where did they take you on the bus when you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact minute, but about 9 o'clock, 9.30, we arrived to the barracks, over there at the fairgrounds. That is where we ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now when you say, "the barracks", do you mean the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this was the JNA barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the same place which was near your home when you described earlier in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the JNA barracks what happened then? Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Different things happened, because I believe we were there for over four hours, standing. Then these good friends of ours and neighbours, the reservists with automatic weapons were going around the buses, threatening. For instance, a neighbour of mine who was in the school of my -- with my daughter, was slapping himself in the back, in his behind where he kept his knife, and making signs like he was going to slit my throat. Some were screaming with joy, as if you were watching a movie and some Indians capture a white man and then you do not know what they would do to him. Then some were lucky. Some were fortunate. Some people came to get some people out, and they even got on to the bus. I remember a mathematics professor named Licina. Then there was Hidek, who had a watchmaker, and another called Kolesar, and then I saw that from some other buses there were people being taken out, and I thought, "lucky them, they are fortunate". However, up front there was a military bus where people were -- they were placing people on that bus and I saw that people were being beaten as this was done, and then I immediately revised my opinion and I thought well, they are not so lucky. Then some people were being taken aside to stay at the barracks, so a little while later, this bus started in the direction of Negoslavci. I did not know where they were taking them, but while they were putting them on this bus some of these young men, these reservists, had broken the anti- -- or the fire extinguishers and they were breaking down some tools like pickaxes and shovels and breaking off the handles with screams and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just during the period of four hours that you said that you were at the JNA barracks, were you inside the bus? Did you stay inside the bus all that time or did you get out at any stage yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You could not leave at all. I spent the entire time on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, these were reservists who were making these threats and were carrying on outside of the bus. Did any of them enter the bus or attempt to enter the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They threatened and they actually tried to get on to the bus, but as I recall, those three men quietly got off the bus. There was no violence, because there were these three soldiers at the door of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "soldiers", do you mean JNA soldiers or reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did they protect the people on the bus from these others that were outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you then moved on and said in your evidence that the buses then moved off, headed towards Negoslavci. What happened then? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First was the military one that set off and then followed by this other bus, one by one by one, and the other one, with screens and everything, so we set off in the direction of Negoslavci but we did not know where we were going. Instead of going to Negoslavci they turned to the left. I am a local from Vukovar and I spent 50 years there. I was never at this Ovcara in Jakobovac. I was never in agriculture so I did not know where we were going. I did not know this place. And then we arrived at Ovcara. Some people on the bus said so, and so that is what I learned, that this place was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you first arrived at Ovcara, was your bus still the number 4 bus, fourth bus back in the row or had it changed positions after leaving the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the buses remained in their positions. I do not recall them changing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when they pulled up at Ovcara where did they pull up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They pulled up next to a building, a hall of sorts, and as these buses were unloading people, they would move off all in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the buses would line up one after the other, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did the people on the buses on all of the buses get out at once or did they get out at one bus at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One bus at a time. I remember that Goran Mogosa, my neighbour three doors away from me, his nickname was Kustra, he was the one that we had to report to first so that he would take everything from you. Bags, wallets, jewellery. He would strip you of everything. I am not sure that he was able to search everyone. When my turn came, he did not take much from me. He took my watch and he took some German marks. But around him there were a lot of bags, suitcases, briefcases; personal documents, jackets, strewn clothes. He was standing next to a ditch. So there were -- it was about 3 square metres, this area, and this was all filled with -- piled with things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when people got off the buses, what happened to them apart from having to surrender their wallets and watches and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then you had to go about 5, 6 or 3 metres, depending on the person where people were coming from. He did not have the time to strip people of all these belongings and then you had to step into what I would call hell. They beat you from all sides, kicking, fists, hands, boots. I remember they got to Damjan Samardzic with these sticks and everything and they beat him up. He never moved again after that. And there was another one. I think it was his nephew, Gaso. In any event, two bodies remained there lying for over two hours. I personally, I received two blows. Once in the crotch and once in the stomach then once a fist in my jaw and then there was a man from Negoslavci. He said, "do you know him?", and I turned around and one hit me so hard with a stick, actually, you know, it is like a crutch that one has or one uses when wounded, and he hit me so hard that I immediately started bleeding. Then I went, and then I -- fortunately I was not felled by this blow, so I went into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the people that were doing the beating outside of the hangar, did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the hangar, as I said, there was this Goran Mogosa, called Kustro, who was taking these things and my neighbour, Stevan Zoric. He lived in Dalmatinska Street. He is a neighbour of mine from the house in -- near the barracks. I am not sure about his sons because they were younger, but later I learned that they were also at Ovcara, so I assumed that they were there too but I cannot guarantee. Then it was Milos Bulidza. He was a butcher from the hospital. He was also one of the most prominent there. And the others I do not know. I said there were about 12 or 13 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how were these people dressed? Did you see? Were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were also wearing the olive green uniforms, the JNA reservists, like the JNA reservists were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during this beating did you at any stage lose consciousness ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fortunately for me, not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you hit in the eyes at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not hit in the eyes. The blow came across the shoulder and over the head on my right-hand side. Sort of behind my ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your vision otherwise -- in any way otherwise impaired as a result of being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. In fact, you start -- you become more alert in a way. You can see more than you normally see. In other words, I was not bothered in any way, but I was fortunate that they were too busy with Damjan Samardzic so that I fared rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that you managed to make your way into the hangar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I ran inside. I did not walk inside, I ran inside. When I came inside, I immediately saw many men, you know, I knew some of them, some of them were my friends. Some I made furniture for, they had arrived at Ovcara before us. That was Ante Podruzjo, Zeljko Begov, Stanko Posavec, the Kolak brothers. They were so beaten up, they were so swollen that Zeljko Begov, who was next to me, fainted several times, and we tried to revive him several times. These were the men who had arrived before us in that military bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the JNA or reservist persons inside the hangar when you went inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That at that moment everybody was still wearing the JNA uniforms and I already said whom I saw outside, but five or six minutes later some people were still coming inside. The president of the municipality, Slavko Dokmanovic, there was a young wounded man who was crouching facing the entrance and Slavko Dokmanovic hit him. He kicked him fully in the face and five or six minutes after that, another young man ran inside. He was about 18, 17, 19, I do not know how old. A friend of mine was looking for a son of his, Tomislav Panis. He looked like his father but I am not sure that I could say that that was him. Whoever knows about Sokar, he know what scissors are. He came in and, following Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you, did Slavko Dokmanovic say anything to anyone when he came into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall and my memory still serves me, after me, Emil Cakalic showed up and his employee, he was the sanitary inspector --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "his employee", whose employee did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I did not say -- well, I said Slavko Dokmanovic was president of the assembly, so how should I put it, he was the major of the city. And Emil Cakalic worked for the municipality together with Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And tell us; what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since Cakalic too entered, then he sort of ironically said, "Oh, Mr. Inspector, you are here too". So that those who were inside, you know, the reservists, that is -- surrounded him and fell upon him and he again had gotten quite a bit -- he had received some beatings outside but now he received more. I forgot to say that first Cakalic got beaten and then he took this -- then he hit this young one with this scissor type of kick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who hit the young one with the scissor-type kick? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President of the municipality, Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who used the words, "Oh, Mr. Inspector, you are here too"? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how far away from Mr. Cakalic were you when Mr. Dokmanovic spoke to him? How far in distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 4 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you able to hear the conversation clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, that is what he said. He did not speak quietly. He also told him something later, but there was confusion around so I could not hear it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In all, how long in periods of time was Mr. Dokmanovic in the room, in the hangar there where you could see him yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to add that Sinisa Glavasevic was there too. He was a reporter from Vukovar for Zagreb. I could not see him. He was quite far away, but they fell upon him so much that I could not see him so I did not give any statement, but when they found him at Ovcara, now I am rewinding the tape, and I am saying that was him. In terms of time, timewise, Slavko Dokmanovic was there for about 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that Slavko Dokmanovic was there, did you have a good view of him? Were you able to see him clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very clearly. Very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the lighting like in the hangar at that time when he came in, when Slavko Dokmanovic came in? What was the lighting like in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see Slavko Dokmanovic in the full facial view of him or did you only see him on the side or did you see both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I saw him very clearly facing me because there were not that many people yet inside. I am not one of the shortest people, I am not one of the tallest people, but I saw him at a distance of about 4 or 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to that time, how long had you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you a precise answer. Now it has been six or seven years, but I have known him for over 20 years, because he used to play soccer. He played soccer, and he also went to soccer games and I knew him from sight. I know about 20,000 people in Vukovar. I do not know everybody's last name. I also saw him later at Pik because, you know, I also had carpet stamping business as well and there is some curtains I once put up there in Pik. So I knew him from sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was Pik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an agricultural, industrial corporation. It is a very large company. I do not know how much land they had, how much livestock, hogs, pigs they had, so it was a food industry company, so it was all part of this Pik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where was this located, this Pik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will make it easier for you. If we are here in The Hague, let us say seven kilometres to the east, seven kilometres to the west, 10 kilometres to the south, there were villages of Negoslavci, so the -- Ilok, Ilok was 35 kilometres away from Vukovar. Trpinja, from where Slavko Dokmanovic is, Bobota, so those are a large stretches of land. So from Vukovar you could go 35 kilometres in each direction and that would be all part of the Pik. Even some vineyards were there, and they belonged to the Pik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, why was it that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic at the Pik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was just by chance that I saw him. I was hanging up curtains or maybe washing carpets. He came by. As far as I know he worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And apart from seeing him previously at the Pik, did you see him from time to time when he became mayor of the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not so frequently, but it would happen that I would go to the town hall to settle an account or something, so one would come across him. I cannot say that I saw him once in three weeks. Sometimes I would not see him for six or seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now would you look around this courtroom and see if you can see Slavko Dokmanovic in the courtroom, and if you can, would you point to him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen him. He is in the last row on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, going back to the time when you saw Slavko Dokmanovic at the hangar in Ovcara, did you notice at all how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the only one who was dressed in a blue pilot uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he have a coat or anything above the uniform or was it just the plain uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had some kind of a jacket but it was not buttoned up, like a wind jacket or something to protect him from the rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what colour was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to this jacket, or his suit underneath?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, the jacket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more like navy blue or close to black. But navy blue. A bit lighter. The suit was a bit lighter but that was also dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the clothes that he had on, did you see whether or not there was any insignia or military markings on these clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not Slavko Dokmanovic was armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I saw him, no. He was not armed. He did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And now I think you have already touched in your evidence upon some of the things that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic do, but what was he doing for that period of 20 minutes that he was in the hangar? Can you tell us? You have already told us some of the things that he was doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was walking up and down rather nervously for as long as there was some room inside, and in those twenty minutes he hit those two men. He gave Cakalic a rather hard slap, and I cannot say for sure what he said about Sinisa Glavasevic, who was to the right when you go into the hangar. I was quite far away so I could not really see but I saw somebody being beaten. I did not know who it was, I just saw that there was a crowd there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened next? What happened -- what was the next thing to happen after you observed what Slavko Dokmanovic was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a reservist of some 40, quite strong -- and he had a whistle like the judges have at football matches. Some people were getting beaten inside, and after about 10 minutes the door was opened a little. They were not closed. This reservist came in and whistled, and said, "that is enough. Let us go". I can tell you that I personally was glad. However, one set went out and another set came in. I was not beaten again, but others did get some beatings. There were two women in that hall too. I know one of them. Dragica Tuskan. I do not know the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you subsequently become separated from the rest of the group in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, roughly, shall we say about an hour and a half later of what I would describe as hell, I do not think hell is like that, though I have never been to hell. I do not really know whom I should thank for staying alive, because Ivankovic was there, then my neighbour Stevan Zoric. I got on well with Puric, even. We played soccer together. In any event, I was taken 22 out with, I would say, about ten others. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) I do not know his surmame. Then somebody called Joakim Dudas, around -- I cannot recall any more names. I think there were about 10 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were separated, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took us out, after about 20 minutes we were outside. Suddenly it became dark, and then we entered a kind of combi Polo. I remember well that the lights had to be turned down because as we started there was another vehicle coming towards us with its lights on. They took us as far as Velepromet and there was no room there. So, then they took us to a knitwear plant known as Modateks. It is on the road between Petrovci and Vukovar. We got there, shall we say, about 6.30, 7 o'clock. I do not know exactly, because I no longer had my watch on me and believe me, I had forgotten that I had a pocket watch as well. The only thing that the Mogosa did not take from me. You know how it is, it was the winter time, I was wearing a jacket so I had several pockets and he simply did not find that watch. And so, about 7 o'clock, 7.30, we reached Modateks. At the door was George Japavlovic. Until yesterday, a bricklayer who had been -- who had worked on my house or rather my son-in-law's house, and talking to him was a woman. As far as I know she is Croatian, Nevenka, just now I cannot recall the surname, but I will remember later on in my testimony. Abramovic. And there was a light from the left, a rather dim light, and below that light I would say there were about 120 or 140 women to the left, so we entered this big factory hall straight ahead, and no more than five minutes later a man, somebody called Dusko, a good-looking young man, a Serb, who used to work in the iron works and as it was quite dark, he asked

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: you. We will talk in the morning". And that was all that happened that evening on 20th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, so by now it is 21st November, about 5 am, I am not quite sure, three buses, I think, and the women were taken away. Again, I do not know where to, and we stayed behind alone. In the morning, some regular JNA soldiers appeared. There were some reservists as well, and the most important among them was somebody known as Deda. I know him well but I do not know his name. I cannot say anything bad about him. You will hear later on about him in my testimony. But about 8.30 it was raining outside, and I know I must have done -- I do not know, I must have done something wrong, since they told me to go and collect the rainwater because it was raining, in a can. I did not even have time to feel afraid, and this young soldier took out a pistol and fired behind my back. I did not bat an eyelid, so I started washing this large hall and about 10 o'clock, 10.30, a young girl, not more than fifteen, sixteen, shall we say, appeared dressed in an olive green uniform with a coat, a JNA overcoat, with two soldiers and she pointed her finger at me and then the two of them took me against the wall. They spread my arms. She had a knife of some 20 centimetres long, and she put it against my neck. I did not know who she was. The first question was, "who did you vote for?"; do not expect me to be brave. I said, "Ivica Racen". He was the Communist, because Yugoslavia was a Communist country. "Who else did you vote for?", she said. I said, "for Milicovic", I think he is from Bobota. He was director of the Post Office. He was the municipal delegate. And another one of ours who was also a local from Vukovar, and then she said, "how many Serbs have you killed?", "how many old women have you killed?", "where is your uniform?". And, "where is your automatic rifle?". Believe me, I was not that scared as I was at Ovcara. So I said, "what do you mean?". Then she shouted at me. She took a cigarette from this soldier. She approached four centimetres to my eye, and she wanted to put out the cigarette in my eye. I do not know whether she would have succeeded but the young soldier would not let her do it. After that, the situation calmed down a little. But I wish to emphasise on 21st of November while those women were still there, some women, because I do not think all of the women were there. This particular soldier, using an anti-aircraft gun, fired so much in the yard so that the other one told us, "do not be afraid, it is my friend's patron saint's day". I never knew what day that was. So, the situation calmed down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I interrupt the evidence for one moment and ask that there be a redaction of page 149, lines 12 and 13? Thank you. Mr. Berghofer, were you subsequently taken, imprisoned in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr, Doctor, this is still 21st. We have not reached Velepromet yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Well, perhaps you could, in a summary form, tell us how it is that you ultimately ended up in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall speed it up. Around 2 o'clock (redacted)-- he cursed my mother and said, "who brought you here?". Perkovic said, "Ivankovic", and I do not know who else he mentioned. He cursed his mother again, and ours and said he was going to kill him first and then us. I am not sure, and I did not hear well. I have already fixed the number of them, but I am not sure about that. In any event, this Deda gave us some bread and then Jesda, Mistankovic appeared and he too is a neighbour who never hurt me and accompanied by Deda, Jesda Mistankovic and another one, they took us to Velepromet. In Velepromet they separated Perkovic, Tihomir. One of them kicked him in the face, took him out, cursed his mother, threatening to cut his ear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)and about 2300 hours, two young soldiers came and said, "do not be afraid, the captain wants to save you, so get on the bus", and we went off to the barracks somewhere just before midnight on 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean from the barracks? So it is already 22nd now. Yes. They registered our names. They put us on the buses, and we were driven off direct to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long were you imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you then subsequently exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. I was exchanged on 27th March 1992. Near Osijek at Nemetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions, your Honour, but before cross-examination, might I ask for another redaction at page 154, line 11? That has been notified to the Registry. If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I turn to Mr. Fila and ask whether he would like to start because it is rather late. It is twenty past five. We should, in principle, stop at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot finish by 5.30 under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But do you prefer to start tomorrow morning at 9.15? Probably it is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It would be better, but if you wish, I can take advantage of the remaining ten minutes, but it would be better to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I think it is better to adjourn until tomorrow at 9.15 sharp. So we stand in recess. (5.20 pm)
